title: Why big data systems exist, and when you don't need one
goal: By the end you can say what kind of work batch systems exist for, estimate how long a full scan takes from bytes and bandwidth, name the two levers that make it faster (more readers, fewer bytes), and decide whether a workload needs a cluster at all.

warmup.q: A finance report needs a full scan of a 1 TB CSV export that sits on one SSD reading 500 MB/s. About how long does the scan take?
options: It depends mostly on how clever the SQL is
warmup.why: 1 TB is 1,000,000 MB. At 500 MB/s that is 2,000 seconds, about 33 minutes. A report that needs every row has to read every byte, so the SQL can't make the scan smaller. Only fewer bytes or more bandwidth can.

sections.h: A full scan costs bytes divided by bandwidth
sections.body:
This track is about **batch processing**: jobs that read a large, fixed input from start to end and compute a result from it, such as a settlement report, a reconciliation or a backfill. The Stream processing track dealt with input that never ends. A batch job's input is complete before the job starts, so the first question is how long reading all of it takes.

Finance asks for one number per merchant: total settled volume for last quarter. Think about what a program has to do to answer that. It has to look at every payment in the quarter, take its merchant and its amount, and add the amount to that merchant's total. Every row, once. Reading every row of a table, or of the slice a query asks about, is called a **full scan**.

Here is one row, as a line in a CSV file of made-up payments that you'll generate in a minute:

```text
0,2026-10-01 00:00:00,3352,FR,GBP,191136,AUTHORIZED,5037,0.3146,cfcd208495d565ef
```

That line is about 85 bytes. Ten million such lines make an 846 MB file. A scan has to move all 846 MB from the disk into memory and through the CPU, so its main cost is easy to write down:

```text
scan time = bytes read / bandwidth
```

**Bandwidth** is how many bytes per second one stage of the trip can move. A scan passes through several stages: the disk, sometimes a network link, and the CPU, which has to turn bytes into numbers and strings. The slowest stage sets the speed of the whole trip, like the narrowest pipe in a line of pipes. Here are round numbers worth remembering. Vendors count in decimal, so 1 MB is 1,000,000 bytes, 1 GB is 1,000 MB and 1 TB is 1,000,000 MB.

| Reader | Streams about | 1 TB takes |
|---|---|---|
| A hard disk | 200 MB/s | 83 minutes |
| A SATA SSD | 500 MB/s | 33 minutes |
| A laptop NVMe SSD | 3 GB/s | 6 minutes |
| A 10 Gb/s network link | 1.25 GB/s | 13 minutes |
| One CPU core parsing CSV | 0.7 GB/s (you'll measure it) | 24 minutes |

Your payment services rarely meet this formula. When a service loads one authorization by its id, the database uses an index. An index is a sorted lookup structure, like the index at the back of a book, that lets the database jump straight to the page holding that row. That takes about a millisecond however big the table is. Finance's question needs every row of the quarter, and no index makes "every row" smaller. So its cost grows with the data: 846 MB takes a second or two, 1 TB takes 33 minutes on a SATA SSD.

That growth is the problem big data systems were built for, and Google hit it first. Its 2004 MapReduce paper mentions disks that read about 30 MB/s. At that speed one disk needs more than 9 hours to read 1 TB once, and the paper says a typical job processed many terabytes.

The figure below is the picture for the whole track: bytes to read on the left, the readers that move them in the middle, the time on the right. There are only two ways to make the time smaller. Add readers (section 2), or shrink the bytes (section 3).

To measure the formula on your laptop you'll use DuckDB. DuckDB is a query engine (a program that runs SQL over data) that lives inside your own process on one machine, much like SQLite but built for scans. It reads CSV files directly, and also Parquet, a file format that stores data column by column, which section 3 explains.

try.title: Time one core reading a CSV file
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the command below. The first run writes 10 million made-up payments to `bigdata/build/l01/`, as CSV (846 MB) and as Parquet (393 MB). That takes about 10 seconds. Later runs reuse the files.
Before you read the output, guess: does one CPU core read the CSV faster or slower than a SATA SSD's 500 MB/s?
Read the speed it prints and the 1 TB estimate. Run it twice more and see how much the number moves.

code.title: ScanDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.batch.l01.demo

/** Times one CPU core scanning a CSV file, then turns that speed into "how long for 1 TB". */
fun main() {
    PaymentFiles.open().use { c ->
        c.createStatement().use { it.execute("SET threads = 1") }        // one reader, like one disk
        val csv = PaymentFiles.csv
        val sql = "SELECT count(*), sum(amount_cents) FROM read_csv('${csv.absolutePath}')"
        val seconds = PaymentFiles.bestSeconds(c, sql)
        val bytesPerSecond = csv.length() / seconds
        println("file:      ${csv.name}, ${PaymentFiles.mb(csv.length())}, %,d rows".format(PaymentFiles.ROWS))
        println("one core:  %.2f s, so about %s per second".format(seconds, PaymentFiles.mb(bytesPerSecond.toLong())))
        println("1 TB at that speed: about %.0f minutes".format(1e12 / bytesPerSecond / 60))
    }
}

try.expect:
On a 12-core Apple Silicon laptop it printed:

```text
file:      payments.csv, 846 MB, 10,000,000 rows
one core:  1.19 s, so about 713 MB per second
1 TB at that speed: about 23 minutes
```

Your speed will differ with your CPU. The file was written seconds ago, so the operating system still holds it in RAM, in its page cache (the Operating systems track's lesson on the page cache), and the SSD barely works. What you measured is how fast one core splits CSV text into fields. The CPU is the slowest stage here, so the CPU sets the bandwidth.

refs.title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters (Dean and Ghemawat, OSDI 2004)

sections.h: Split the bytes across many machines
sections.body:
If one disk needs 2,000 seconds for 1 TB, the obvious fix is more disks. Put half the table on a second disk, read both at once, and the scan takes 1,000 seconds. One machine only holds a few disks, so to go further you need more machines. A group of machines that work on one job together is a **cluster**. Spread the table over 100 machines, 10 GB each, and every machine reads its share in 20 seconds, all at the same time.

Growing by adding machines is called scale-out. The other option, scale-up, means buying one bigger machine. In the early 2000s a bigger machine cost far more and still had only a few disks, so Google built on racks (cabinets) full of cheap PCs. The MapReduce paper describes them: dual-processor x86 boxes with 2 to 4 GB of memory, cheap IDE disks, and network links of 100 Mb/s or 1 Gb/s.

For finance's question, each machine computes a partial answer, the totals per merchant for its own 10 GB, and then someone adds up the 100 partial answers. That someone is a **coordinator**: a program that cuts the work into pieces, starts one task (one piece of work, here "scan this share and total it") on each machine, and combines the results. Now look at what breaks on the way from one machine to a hundred. The stepper below walks through it with the same 1 TB table.

The first problem is startup. The coordinator has to plan the job, start 100 tasks and collect 100 results, and that time doesn't shrink as you add machines. In the paper, a grep (a search for a text pattern) over 1 TB on about 1,800 machines took about 150 seconds, and about a minute of that was startup.

The second problem is the slowest machine. The job is done only when the last share is done. The paper describes a machine whose bad disk slowed its reads from 30 MB/s to 1 MB/s. One machine like that, called a straggler, holds up the other 99.

The third is failure. On one machine a dead disk is rare. With hundreds of cheap machines, says the paper on GFS (Google's file system), component failures are the norm. If a machine dies halfway through, its share must be read again somewhere else, so every share must exist on more than one machine. Lesson 3 of this track shows how Google, and later Hadoop (the open-source copy of Google's design), stored those copies.

Splitting also has a floor. The coordinator doesn't hand out slivers of any size. It hands out fixed-size pieces of a file called blocks. In HDFS (Hadoop's distributed file system) and in Spark (the engine most of this track uses) a block is 128 MiB. MiB means binary megabytes: 128 x 1,048,576 = 134,217,728 bytes. 1 TB is 7,451 such blocks, so a 7,452nd machine has nothing to read. You'll compute all of this in the lab.

frames.say: Side by side: 100 machines reading rows finish in 20 seconds plus startup, if none of them is slow. One machine reading compressed columns finishes in 40 seconds, or 7 on NVMe. Read fewer bytes first, then decide whether you need more readers.

try.title: Add readers on your laptop
steps: Run `ThreadsDemo`. It runs the same CSV scan with DuckDB limited to 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads, then all your cores. A thread is one line of execution inside a program, and each one can run on its own CPU core. Here each thread scans its own chunks of the file, like machines scanning their own blocks.
Predict first: with 8 threads, is it 8 times faster than with 1?
Compare the speedup column with your core count.

code.title: ThreadsDemo.kt

try.expect:
On the same 12-core laptop:

```text
 1 threads: 1.18 s   speedup 1.0x
 2 threads: 0.63 s   speedup 1.9x
 4 threads: 0.34 s   speedup 3.4x
 8 threads: 0.20 s   speedup 5.8x
12 threads: 0.18 s   speedup 6.4x
```

The speedup grows, but slower than the thread count. DuckDB still has to split the file and combine the partial sums, many laptop chips mix fast and slow cores, and every thread shares one memory bus. A cluster flattens out the same way, with the network in place of the memory bus.

sections.h: Read fewer bytes before you add machines
sections.body:
Look at the CSV line again. Finance needs two of its ten fields: the merchant (`3352`) and the amount (`191136`). The scan still reads all 85 bytes. In a CSV file the fields of one row sit next to each other, and the next row starts only after the last field of this one. So the reader can't jump from one amount to the next. It has to walk through every byte of every line. Storing each row's values together like this is a **row layout**.

The fix is to store the table the other way round: all payment ids first, then all timestamps, then all merchants, and so on. (The comparison box after the sections shows the same three rows both ways.) Now a query that needs two columns reads two runs of values and skips the other eight. Storing each column's values together is a columnar layout. The Storage track's lesson on column stores built it inside one database; Parquet, the format most of this track uses, is the same idea as a file that any engine can read.

Columns also compress well, because the values in one column look alike. The `currency` column in the demo data holds only four different values. Instead of writing `EUR` ten million times, a file can keep the list `EUR, USD, GBP, INR` once and store a tiny number per row that points into it. The `status` column works the same way. Lesson 5 shows the encodings Parquet uses.

The third way to read less is to skip data that can't match. If the table is stored in one folder per day, a question about last week opens seven folders and ignores the rest (lesson 4). If each file records the smallest and largest timestamp inside it, a reader can skip whole files whose range can't match (lesson 5).

Put the three together on the 1 TB table. Say it has 30 columns and finance needs 3 of them, which make up a tenth of each row. Stored by column, the query reads 100 GB. If those columns compress 5 times, it reads 20 GB. At 500 MB/s that is 40 seconds on one machine. On a laptop NVMe SSD at 3 GB/s it is about 7 seconds.

| Plan | Bytes read | Time |
|---|---|---|
| One machine, row layout | 1 TB | 2,000 s |
| 100 machines, row layout | 10 GB each | 20 s plus startup |
| One machine, columns, compressed | 20 GB | 40 s (7 s on NVMe) |

Against SATA SSDs the hundred machines still win on paper, 20 seconds to 40. Against a laptop NVMe they lose. And they cost a hundred machines, while the columnar plan costs a file format. **Shrink the bytes first, then decide whether you need more readers.** Every engine in this track, Spark included, works hard to read less before it reads faster.

try.title: Count the bytes each format reads
steps: Run `FewerBytesDemo`. It asks for `count(*)` and `sum(amount_cents)` from the CSV, then reads all ten columns of the Parquet file, then asks the first question of the Parquet file.
Predict the bytes read for each line before you look. Does the CSV query read only two columns' worth?
Compare the `read` column with the file sizes on the first line.

code.title: FewerBytesDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
files: csv 846 MB, parquet 393 MB
csv, 2 columns      read 988.2 MB in 0.194s
parquet, all 10     read 390.7 MB in 0.120s
parquet, 2 columns  read 47.7 MB in 0.0089s
```

The CSV query reads the whole file, and DuckDB even counts a little more than its size. It needs two columns, but in a row layout the other eight columns sit between the values you want, so the reader has to go through them. Parquet with all ten columns reads about its file size. The two-column Parquet query reads 48 MB, about 5% of the CSV. DuckDB answers `count(*)` from the row counts Parquet stores inside the file, and reads only the compressed `amount_cents` column. The times are tiny because both files sit in the page cache. From a cold SSD or from S3, the bytes decide the time.

sections.h: Most data fits on one machine
sections.body:
So how big is "big"? The What data systems are for track's lesson on growing past one machine made the general case with the COST paper: a cluster first has to beat one good single-threaded program on the same problem, and published systems often needed hundreds of cores to do that, or never managed it. Here is the same question in this lesson's terms.

Jordan Tigani was a founding engineer on Google BigQuery, a cloud data warehouse that runs SQL over very large tables. In his 2023 post "Big Data is Dead" he looked at how customers actually used it. Most customers had less than 1 TB of data in total. Among customers spending more than $1,000 a year, 90% of queries processed less than 100 MB. His figures come from one product, and he calls them approximate. They still match what most backend teams see: your ledger might hold a few hundred GB, and the queries people run read last week's slice of it.

Put his numbers into this lesson's formula. 100 MB at the 0.7 GB/s that one core parses CSV is about a seventh of a second. Even the 1 TB table from section 3, read as 3 compressed columns out of 30, is 20 GB: under 10 seconds on one NVMe disk. For most questions most companies ask, one machine is enough.

So when do you need a cluster? When the bytes a job must read, after skipping everything it can, are more than one machine can scan in your time budget. Think multi-terabyte daily loads, backfills (recomputing results over years of past events), joins between two huge tables, and feature pipelines for fraud models. You also need one when a job runs for hours and has to survive a machine failing halfway, or when many teams and tools share one copy of the data. Spark, the engine most of this track uses, exists for those cases. Even Spark agrees about the rest: Spark 4.3 added an opt-in setting, `spark.sql.optimizer.singleTaskExecution.enabled`, that runs small queries as a single task instead of spreading them over the cluster.

The track follows the same order. Lesson 2 runs a whole batch job on one machine with Unix tools and shows the two ways any engine groups data: hashing and sorting. Lessons 3 to 8 spread that job over many machines: a distributed file system and MapReduce, SQL tables over directories of files, columnar files, then Spark's execution model, its shuffle and its optimizer. Lessons 9 to 12 cover Spark 4 from the JVM, warehouses and star schemas, and lakehouse tables. The last three cover orchestration, what batch output is for, and how to choose an engine, with DuckDB on one machine as a real option every time.

refs.title: Big Data is Dead (Jordan Tigani, MotherDuck)
Scalability! But at what COST? (McSherry, Isard and Murray, HotOS 2015)

analogy: Picture a warehouse inventory: count every red shirt. One person walking every aisle takes all day. A hundred people taking one aisle each finish in minutes. Add the time for a foreman to hand out aisles and add up a hundred notes, and the count still waits for whoever got the messiest aisle. Or you store shirts by colour, and one person walks only the red aisle. The analogy breaks in one place: in a warehouse you can see where the red shirts are. A data file has to be built that way on purpose (by column, by date, with statistics), or the engine must read everything to find out.
in_your_world: Every night a Temporal workflow in your settlement service reads yesterday's captured authorizations from Oracle and builds files per acquirer. Say that's 4 million rows at 200 bytes: 800 MB. A full scan at a few hundred MB/s takes seconds, so this is not a big data problem, even when it fails at 2 a.m. The problem appears when finance asks for the same report over three years: about 4.4 billion rows, close to 900 GB in Oracle's row format. That is the moment to export the needed columns to Parquet once and query them on one machine. It is not yet the moment to buy a cluster. (All numbers here are made up for the example.)
mistake: The common mistake is sizing a job by the size of the table instead of the bytes the query reads. A team hears "the ledger is 4 TB" and asks for a Spark cluster. But the ledger covers three years, and the reports read 4 of its 60 columns for the last 30 days: about 7 GB before compression. The opposite mistake is just as common: timing a query twice on a laptop, getting the fast second run from the page cache, and assuming production storage reads that fast. Both have the same fix. Write down the bytes read after skipping columns and partitions, take the bandwidth of the slowest stage on the real hardware, and divide.

compare.title: The same three payments, by row and by column

b.label: Column layout (Parquet, simplified)
b.title: payments.parquet
b.src:
payment_id       0 | 1 | 2
created_at       2026-10-01 00:00:00 | 2026-10-17 08:52:32 | 2026-10-08 21:40:34
merchant_id      3352 | 3834 | 3982
card_country     FR | BR | US
currency         GBP | EUR | EUR
amount_cents     191136 | 170792 | 178237
status           AUTHORIZED | CAPTURED | DECLINED
mcc              5037 | 5446 | 5369
fraud_score      0.3146 | 0.5569 | 0.7361
idempotency_key  cfcd208495d565ef | c4ca4238a0b92382 | c81e728d9d4c2f63

compare.note: Both hold the same payments from the demo files. To compute `sum(amount_cents)` from the CSV, the reader goes through every line and splits out the sixth field. In the column layout, all amounts sit together, so the reader fetches that one run of values and skips the other nine. Values in a column also look alike (the same three currencies, statuses from a short list), which is why columns compress so well. Real Parquet first cuts the rows into chunks called row groups and stores each chunk column by column. At the end of the file, in the footer, it keeps an index of where every column starts. Lesson 5 opens one up.

worked.title: Size a fraud backfill before you book a cluster

steps.say: A fraud analyst wants a velocity feature recomputed over 18 months of authorizations: about 2.2 billion rows in Oracle, roughly 200 bytes each. First, describe the data as it sits today. The backfill needs four columns; lump the rest together.
Next, work out the bytes the job reads, as rows and as compressed columns. Assume Parquet compresses these columns 4 times; you'll check real ratios in lesson 5.
steps.code:
// 2. bytes read: the row store drags all 200 bytes along
val need = setOf("card_id", "merchant_id", "amount_cents", "created_at")
val rowBytes = ScanMath.bytesRead(asRows, need)                         // 440 GB
val asParquet = asRows.copy(layout = Layout.COLUMNAR, compressionRatio = 4.0)
val columnBytes = ScanMath.bytesRead(asParquet, need)                   // 15.4 GB

steps.say: Then time both plans on hardware you could actually get: one VM with a 3 GB/s NVMe disk, or a 20-node cluster of 500 MB/s SATA SSDs with 30 seconds of startup.

Decide. The single machine wins by an order of magnitude because it reads 28 times fewer bytes. The expensive step is the one-time export of 440 GB out of Oracle, so do that once, keep the Parquet files, and run every later backfill against them.

lab.title: Build a back-of-the-envelope scan calculator
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the tests once. All nine fail with `NotImplementedError`. The first run downloads Spark and DuckDB for the whole track, so give it a minute.
Write `scanSeconds` and `blockCount`. Keep `blockCount` in `Long` arithmetic: one test feeds it 10 PB in 1-byte blocks.
Write `clusterSeconds`. The busiest machine gets `ceil(blocks / machines)` blocks, but never more bytes than the file has. Startup is added once.
Write `bytesRead`. A `ROW` table reads every column whatever the query needs. Reject unknown columns first.
Write `machinesNeeded` with a plain loop over machine counts. Return `null` when even one block per machine is too slow.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then read the test names from top to bottom: together they are this lesson's argument.
hints: Ceiling division with integers is `(a + b - 1) / b`. It stays exact for any `Long` this lab uses.
In `bytesRead`, multiply before you divide: `Math.round(rows.toDouble() * bytesPerRow / compressionRatio)`.
More machines than blocks can't help, so the loop in `machinesNeeded` can stop at `blockCount(bytes, blockSize)`.

drill.title: Estimate a cluster scan from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. A 5 TB table of settlement events sits as CSV on 40 machines with 200 MB/s disks, in 128 MiB blocks, and the job has 45 seconds of startup. On paper, how long does a full scan take? Then write `clusterSeconds` from memory and check your number with it.

recap: A full scan costs the bytes read divided by the bandwidth of the slowest stage: disk, network or CPU decoding. 1 TB at 500 MB/s is 2,000 seconds.
Scale-out splits the bytes across machines. It adds startup, waits for the slowest machine, and has to survive failures.
Parallelism stops at the number of pieces: 1 TB in 128 MiB blocks is at most 7,451 tasks.
Reading fewer bytes (columns, compression, skipping files) is the cheaper lever. Pull it before you add machines.
Most companies' data, and most queries, fit on one machine. Do the arithmetic before you pick Spark.

quiz.q: A nightly job reads 600 GB of Parquet files from object storage (a file service reached over the network, such as Amazon S3). The VM pulls 1.5 GB/s from storage and decodes Parquet at 4 GB/s. Roughly how long does the scan take?
quiz.why: The slowest stage sets the bandwidth, and here that's storage: 600 GB at 1.5 GB/s is 400 seconds, about 7 minutes. The tempting 2.5 minutes uses the decode speed, but the CPU can only decode bytes that have arrived.

quiz.q: A 2 GB file is stored in 128 MiB blocks, one task per block. You run a scan on a cluster with 50 idle machines. How many machines do any work?
quiz.why: 2,000,000,000 / 134,217,728 = 14.9, so the file has 15 blocks and the scan has 15 tasks. The other 35 machines wait. The tempting 16 comes from dividing by 128,000,000 instead of 128 MiB, and 50 assumes work splits as finely as you like.

quiz.q: A table has 40 columns of similar width. A query needs 4 of them. You move the table from CSV to a columnar format that compresses 4 times. Roughly how many fewer bytes does the query read?
options: No change, because a query reads whole rows either way
quiz.why: Reading 4 of 40 columns cuts the bytes 10 times, and compression cuts them 4 times more: 40 times fewer. "10 times" forgets compression. A columnar format exists exactly so that a query doesn't read whole rows.

quiz.q: You double the machines on a scan job and the run time barely changes. Which explanation fits best?
options: Startup or one slow machine already dominated the time
The files are in a columnar format
Each machine now reads fewer blocks
quiz.why: Doubling machines halves only the part of the job that splits: the reading. Startup is paid once, and the job waits for its slowest machine, so if those dominate, more machines don't help. Fewer blocks per machine is what should have made it faster; it just wasn't the bottleneck.

quiz.q: A team stores 300 GB of payment events. Analysts query the last 7 days, about 6 GB, a few times an hour. What should they try first?
options: A 20-node Spark cluster, so queries stay fast as the data grows
Keep the CSV files and buy a machine with more cores
Load everything into a Kafka topic with long retention
Partition by day in a columnar format and query it with a single-machine engine such as DuckDB
quiz.why: The queries read about 6 GB, less after column pruning and compression. One machine scans that in seconds. A cluster adds startup, cost and operations for a problem that isn't there yet. More cores help CSV a little, but reading fewer bytes helps far more.

flashcards.front: What is your first estimate for a full scan's time?
flashcards.back: Bytes read divided by the bandwidth of the slowest stage (disk, network or CPU decoding). 1 TB at 500 MB/s is 2,000 s.

flashcards.front: Why can't 10,000 machines scan a 1 TB HDFS file faster than 7,451 machines can?
flashcards.back: Work comes in 128 MiB blocks, one task each. 1 TB is 7,451 blocks, so extra machines have nothing to read.

flashcards.front: What does scale-out cost besides the extra machines?
flashcards.back: Startup and coordination that don't shrink, waiting for the slowest machine, and re-running work when a machine fails.

flashcards.front: A query needs 3 of 30 equally wide columns and the format compresses 5x. What fraction of a 1 TB row scan does it read?
Why is the second run of a scan on your laptop often much faster than the first?
flashcards.back: The OS page cache keeps the file in RAM, so the second run reads memory instead of the SSD.

flashcards.front: What did Tigani report about BigQuery query sizes?
flashcards.back: Among customers spending over $1,000 a year, 90% of queries processed less than 100 MB.

terms.plain: Reading every row of a table (or of the part a query needs), as analytics queries do.
How many bytes per second a stage can move: a disk, a network link, or a CPU decoding a file.
Making one machine bigger: more cores, memory and disks.
Adding machines and splitting the work between them.
The slowest machine or task in a parallel job. The job can't finish before it does.
Storing each column's values together, so a query reads only the columns it names.
Memory where the operating system keeps recently read file data, so the next read skips the disk.

explain_back.prompt: Your manager asks whether the payments team needs a Spark cluster for a new reporting store: 2 TB today, growing 50 GB a month, with dashboards that read the last 30 days. Answer with numbers.
explain_back.answer: Not yet. The size that matters is what the dashboards read, not what we store. Thirty days is about 50 GB at today's rate. Stored in a columnar format and split by day, a dashboard that needs 5 of 40 columns reads about an eighth of that, roughly 6 GB. With 4x compression that's about 1.5 GB. One machine with an NVMe disk streams that in under a second. A cluster would add startup time, a slowest-machine problem and operations work, and buy us nothing at this size. I'd revisit if a single query must read many terabytes, or if jobs run for hours and need to survive machine failures.

deeper.body:
Why did a minute of startup matter so much for Google's grep? Because the part of a job that doesn't split puts a ceiling on the speedup. This is Amdahl's law, and the scan formula makes it concrete.

Take the 1 TB scan at 500 MB/s with 60 seconds of fixed startup. On one machine it takes 60 + 2,000 = 2,060 seconds. On *n* machines it takes 60 + 2,000 / *n*. However large *n* gets, it never drops below 60 seconds, so the speedup can never beat 2,060 / 60, about 34 times. With 100 machines you already get 2,060 / 80, about 26 times. The other 1,700 machines buy the last few times.

Object storage adds a twist. Amazon S3, and services like it, keep files as named objects that you fetch over HTTP. Reading a file from S3 is a series of HTTP requests, and each request has latency (tens of milliseconds) before the first byte arrives. One request at a time gives poor throughput, so engines issue many range requests at once and keep many requests in flight per file. That is why DuckDB 2.0 added asynchronous I/O for Parquet and CSV reads aimed at object storage. The formula still holds; the bandwidth term just depends on how many requests you keep busy.
